⚙️ Under the hood · Step 7 of 8 · 7 min

Cross-entropy by hand

The usual loss of neural classifiers and language models, and perplexity.

🎯 A classifier answers with probabilities

A neural classifier gives every class a score, called a logit, and softmax turns the logits into probabilities. For a photo and the classes cat, dog and fox, the answer might be p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1).

The loss has to say in one number how bad this answer is. It should be small when the true class (what the photo really shows) gets a high probability. The usual choice is the cross-entropy: minus the natural logarithm (ln) of the probability given to the true class.

L = −ln p(true class)
photo of a cat: L = −ln 0.7 ≈ 0.36
photo of a fox: L = −ln 0.1 ≈ 2.30

The full formula compares the target y with the prediction p: L = −Σ_i y_i·ln p_i. Here y_i is 1 for the true class and 0 for the others, so only one term of the sum is left.

📋 What a probability costs: −ln p

The table shows the loss for different probabilities of the true class. The loss is 0 only when p = 1, and it grows without limit as p falls towards 0.

Being unsure is cheap: 0.69 at p = 0.5. Being confident and wrong is expensive: if the true class got only 0.01, the loss is 4.61.

p (true class)−ln p
10
0.90.11
0.50.69
0.251.39
0.12.30
0.014.61

Every halving of p adds the same amount to the loss, ln 2 ≈ 0.693: falling from 0.02 to 0.01 costs as much as falling from 1 to 0.5.

Task. A model gives the true class the probability 0.5. What is its cross-entropy loss −ln(0.5), to two decimal places?

Show the solution

−ln(0.5) = ln(1 / 0.5) = ln 2 ≈ 0.693, so 0.69. This is the loss of a fifty-fifty answer between two classes: the answer of a model that always says 0.5 and has learned nothing. So a loss that stays near 0.69 in a two-class task is a warning sign.

Task. The loss of a batch is usually the mean loss of its examples. Three examples get the true-class probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 1. What is the mean loss, to two decimal places? Use the table.

Show the solution

(0.69 + 1.39 + 0) / 3 = 2.08 / 3 ≈ 0.69. In exact form: (ln 2 + 2·ln 2 + 0) / 3 = ln 2. The mean is the same as for three fifty-fifty answers, although one answer was perfect: one number does not show how the loss is spread over the examples.

Task. A model gives 0.99 to class A and 0.01 to class B. The true class is B. What is the loss? Use the table.

Show the solution

−ln(0.01) ≈ 4.61. The 0.99 for the wrong class is not in the formula: only the 0.01 of the true class counts. One confident mistake costs more than six fifty-fifty answers together: 6 · 0.69 = 4.14.

🧮 Why not accuracy?

Why not train a model on accuracy itself, the share of right answers? A tiny shift of a weight almost never changes any answer, so accuracy stays the same. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere, and gradient descent gets no direction.

Cross-entropy changes smoothly with the probabilities, so it does give a direction. And together with softmax it has a very simple gradient with respect to the logits z: the prediction minus the target.

∂L/∂z = p − y

y is the one-hot target: 1 for the true class and 0 for the others. With three classes and the first one true, y = (1, 0, 0).

Task. Softmax gives p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1), and the true class is the first one. The gradient of the cross-entropy with respect to the logits is p − y (y is 1 for the true class, 0 for the others). What is the gradient's first component?

Show the solution

Here y = (1, 0, 0): this is the one-hot target. So the first component is 0.7 − 1 = −0.3, and the whole gradient is (−0.3, 0.2, 0.1). A step against this gradient pushes the logit of the true class up and the other two down, each in proportion to its error.

🎲 Perplexity: the loss as a number of choices

A language model is a classifier too. Its classes are all the tokens it can output, its vocabulary, and the true class is the token that really comes next. Its loss L is the mean cross-entropy per token.

Perplexity turns L back into a number of choices: the model is as unsure as if it had to pick among that many equally likely tokens. If the vocabulary has V tokens and the model gives each the same probability, its perplexity is exactly V.

perplexity = e^L
p = 1/V for every token:
L = ln V, perplexity = V

Because of the natural logarithm, L is measured in nats (with a base-2 logarithm it would be bits). A lower perplexity is better, and the smallest possible value is 1, when L = 0.

Task. Perplexity is e raised to the mean cross-entropy. A language model has a mean cross-entropy of ln 4 ≈ 1.39 nats per token. What is its perplexity?

Show the solution

e^(ln 4) = 4. On average the model is as unsure as if it chose among 4 equally likely tokens at every step.

Task. A model that knows nothing yet spreads its probability evenly over a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens. What cross-entropy loss should you see at the very start of training?

Show the answer

Right answer: About 10.8: the natural logarithm of 50,000

With V tokens, each gets p = 1/V, so L = −ln(1/V) = ln V = ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8. (50,000 itself is the perplexity e^L.) This is a quick check of a new training run: if a freshly initialised model starts far from ln V, look for a bug first.

Task. Why do deep learning libraries usually compute the cross-entropy straight from the logits and not from the probabilities after softmax?

Show the answer

Right answer: Because it is numerically more stable: no ln(0) and no overflow of e^z

A tiny probability can be rounded down to exactly 0, and ln(0) makes the loss infinite. A large logit can make e^z overflow. Libraries compute ln p directly from the logits (log-softmax), subtracting the largest logit first. So give such a loss function raw logits, not the output of softmax.

Remember

  • Cross-entropy for one example: L = −ln p(true class). For a batch, take the mean over its examples.
  • A confident mistake is expensive: p = 0.5 costs 0.69, but p = 0.01 costs 4.61.
  • With softmax, the gradient with respect to the logits is p − y: the prediction minus the one-hot target.
  • Perplexity is e^L. A model that knows nothing yet starts near L = ln V, where V is the number of classes or tokens.
